name: SkedPal
tagline: Automatically schedules flexible tasks around calendar commitments

pricing.notes: Official pricing page reviewed; taxes, promotions, and regional pricing may differ.

tiers.name: Core
tiers.limits: 21-day automatic-scheduling window and 1 connected calendar account.
tiers.notes: Annual equivalent verified; current monthly numeric price was not exposed in crawlable public text.

tiers.name: Pro
tiers.limits: 60-day automatic-scheduling window, unlimited calendar accounts, and time tracking.
tiers.notes: Annual equivalent verified; current monthly numeric price was not exposed in crawlable public text.

pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual; only annual numeric prices were publicly exposed; 14-day trial with no card
pricing.hiddenCosts: The $9.95 figure on file is the annual-billing equivalent, not a verified month-to-month price. Core is capped at a 21-day scheduling horizon and 1 calendar account; Pro raises the horizon to 60 days and removes the calendar-account cap.

verdictSummary: The visible automatic scheduling loop is buildable, but a credible replacement needs more than the first screen. SkedPal earns its keep through polish, OS integration, so expect a weekend or multi-day build and a narrower personal scope.
coreLoopDIY: Build a local desktop utility that captures the essential automatic scheduling workflow with keyboard-first controls and local storage.
replacementScope: narrow personal or very small-team substitute
requirements: macOS, Windows, or Linux development machine
Local filesystem access and OS permissions
whatYouLose: calendar-provider edge cases and timezone correctness
whyPeopleStillPay: SkedPal: People keep paying because a utility used dozens of times a day must be instant, predictable, and compatible with every OS update.
ongoingBurden: Track OS permission changes, shortcut conflicts, packaging, code signing, and regressions after system updates.

priorArt.name: ActivityWatch
priorArt.desc: Local-first automatic time tracking with an extensible event model.

alternatives.name: FlowSavvy Free
alternatives.desc: It puts tasks around calendar events for free; the rolling scheduling horizon stops two weeks out.

alternatives.name: Reclaim Lite
alternatives.desc: A free one-week planning horizon for tasks and focus time; long-range plans remain billable.

notes: Useful boundary case: the first 60 percent of SkedPal is approachable, but operating the last 40 percent is the real subscription.
prompt:
Build a deliberately narrow personal substitute for SkedPal, not a full clone.
Use exactly this stack: Tauri 2 + React + TypeScript + SQLite.
Primary job: Build a local desktop utility that captures the essential automatic scheduling workflow with keyboard-first controls and local storage.
Start from an empty folder and create the complete working project.
Make the default mode single-user and private.
Store user data locally unless the core job requires the declared self-hosted database.
Do not add analytics, telemetry, ads, or third-party accounts.
Put every secret and external credential in .env and provide .env.example.
Use realistic sample data that is clearly labelled and easy to delete.
Implement the smallest polished interface that completes the core loop end to end.
Include clear empty, loading, validation, success, and failure states.
Add import and export so the user is not trapped in the app.
Use accessible keyboard navigation, labels, focus states, and sensible contrast.
Validate untrusted input and never log secrets or private file contents.
Deliberately exclude these paid-product advantages: calendar-provider edge cases and timezone correctness; cross-device sync; deep operating-system edge-case coverage.
Do not fake integrations, network effects, proprietary data, model quality, compliance, or security claims.
Where an external API is optional, keep the app useful without it and explain the degraded mode.
Write focused unit tests for the data model and the most important workflow.
Add one end-to-end smoke test that proves the core loop works.
Create a README with setup, permissions, architecture, data location, backup, and limitations.
Add scripts for install, development, test, build, and a production-style local run.
Run the tests and build before finishing, then fix errors rather than merely describing them.
